draft.title: Urbanisation
card: Urbanisation is the growing share of a country's or the world's people who live in cities and towns. It is measured as a percentage, not as a head count.
More than half the world's people now live in urban areas. The share is still rising in most regions.
A city can grow in size without urbanisation if the whole population grows at the same rate. Urbanisation means the urban share goes up.
Urban areas often grow when people move in from rural areas to find jobs, services and education. Natural increase in cities adds to the growth as well.
draft.remember: Urbanisation is a rising urban share of the population, not just a bigger city.

a.q: Which change in a country shows urbanisation?
opts: Urban areas hold 60% of people, up from 50%
The biggest city adds 100 000 more people
Rural areas lose people to a nearby country
Each city street has more people than before
a.why: Urbanisation is a rising share of people in urban areas, so a move from 50% to 60% shows it. A city adding people could happen while the national urban share stays the same, so it does not prove urbanisation.
a.clue: Look for a change in share, not in number.

b.q: In Country X, the population grew from 10 million to 12 million. Urban dwellers grew from 5 million to 6 million. What happened to urbanisation?
opts: It did not rise, as the urban share stayed at 50%
It rose, as the urban population grew by a million
It fell, as the total population grew by 2 million
It rose, as more people lived in cities than before
b.why: Urban share was 5 ÷ 10 = 50% and then 6 ÷ 12 = 50%. The share did not change, so there was no urbanisation even though cities grew. The option about a larger urban population is tempting, but urbanisation is about share.
b.clue: Work out the urban share before and after.

a.best: Urban areas hold 60% of people, up from 50%

b.best: It did not rise, as the urban share stayed at 50%

problems.detail: The distractor 'Rural areas lose people to a nearby country' can itself imply urbanisation. If rural people emigrate and the urban population stays the same, the urban share rises. A careful student could argue for it, so it should be reworded, for example so that urban areas lose people at the same rate.
The right option is the only one that gives percentages or a share. Together with the clue 'Look for a change in share, not in number', a student can pick it without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card and question b are accurate. In question a, the rural-emigration distractor could be defended as showing urbanisation, and the right option is the only one stated as a percentage, which the clue then points straight to.
